One of the first things people will ask about you if you mention that you do calisthenics training is "how many push-ups can you do." It's like asking people how much they can bench, really. Not that doing a lot of push-ups is essential to your health, but it's such an iconic and universal exercise it would be weird if you couldn't do a substantial amount of them. The first part of this guide is how to improve push-ups over the long term, the second part is a collection of tips to immediately improve your performance.

First off, you need to know how to do a push-up. Antranik's video is one of the best I've seen on the subject. I deliberately protract my scapulae at the top part to help train my serratus anterior, but that's an optional thing to improve striking strength. The cadence you use heavily depends on your goals. If you have a military test, I believe they still use 2-1-2 (2 seconds up, pause 1 second, 2 seconds down.) I prefer to do reps quickly and "pull" myself down for the concentric portion of the exercise if I'm going for reps. Write down how many you can do. Doing diamond and wide-grip push-ups will improve your total number of regular push-ups as well. I hate planks, but if you have trouble keeping your body straight throughout your sets, they will help. I save isometrics for the end of the session. Be sure to do push-ups as one of the first exercises in your routine, since you will see better gains in the exercises you do first.

I learned this technique from a USMC recruiter, and it works quite well with comparatively little effort. Max sets suck, but you only have to do them twice for it to be effective. It's simple, immediately after you get out of bed, do one max set (as close to failure as possible without collapsing)of push-ups. Then, take care of all your morning stuff (Should take about 10-20 minutes, you can do more or less time) and do another max set. It's not fancy, but it works.

The second programming technique is called "Greasing the Groove" and is one of the fastest ways to massively improve the amount of push-ups You should begin to really notice the affects in about a month. The main downside is that this protocol will affect your ability to do any pushing exercises in your regular routine. Greasing the groove works particularly well with push-ups, but it can be safely adapted to a lot of exercises, such as chin-ups, the Olympic lifts, and more advanced calisthenics movements. It's not recommended for heavy weighted exercises, since they will place a lot of stress on the body. It works by improving neuromuscular efficiency, not strength, so size gains will be minimal. You shouldn't be exhausted at any point from doing this. Rest days are unnecessary.

To use the GtG protocol, you will need to do between 6-10 sub-maximal sets spread throughout the day, with at least 30 minutes to an hour between sets, and going to between 60-80% capacity. I would measure this in number of push-ups done, so if you can do 20, you would do sets of 12-18. You'll probably need to remove other pushing exercises from your routine to avoid over training, leaving just lower-body work and pulling. Expect considerable improvement in 4-6 weeks, you'll probably be able to do twice as many. As with any sort of of high-volume training, be sure to avoid injury, particularly to your wrists. Warm them up a bit, make sure there's no or very little persistent pain after doing your exercises. Don't be afraid to take a day off, or focus on mobility exercises for a little while. I switch to knuckle push-ups when my wrists start to hurt.

To increase your push-ups without consistent training is difficult (if it wasn't you would be able to do more push-ups) but there are some helpful tricks.

My favorite is to pull my lats down, instead of leaving them in the neutral position. Keep them tight. Which leads to the next tip.

Maintain as much tension throughout your body as possible. If you're partway through the set and begin to feel yourself sagging, tense up that muscle group. The more muscles you activate, the easier the exercise will be. This is known as the principle of radiation, by the way.

Choose a good cadence. While I'm never sure if I'm supposed to be inhaling or exhaling during a push-up, I do try to maintain a good rhythm. I like 1-1-1 and I find it helps me do the most reps. It doesn't hurt to mix this variable up though. I recommend 2-1-2 for optimal strength gains.

If you have a friend, coach, or drill instructor to yell at you, great. You don't need much more motivation than that. If you don't however, be sure to push yourself when your finding your max. This will give you a more accurate number of how many to do when calculating your 60-80% range.

Finally, make sure your form is solid. If it isn't you can't possibly know many you're actually doing.

That's all I've got, if I missed something please let me know in the comments.

Edit: I should point out that outside of official fitness tests, there's surprisingly little benefit to doing a huge amount of push-ups. You won't get huge, you won't get a lot stronger, and upper-body endurance can be built more effectively with a regular strength training routine. This is more for experimentation of bragging rights than anything else.
